I'd start by understanding the product.

My approach would be:
1. 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱
Learn the product, users, business-critical workflows, and major risks.

2. 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲
Identify the scenarios that are repetitive, stable, high-risk, and worth automating.

3. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲
Make sure the application, test data, and environment are reliable enough for automation.

4. 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲
Start with the tests that provide the highest value — not simply the easiest ones to automate.

5. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲
Connect the suite with CI/CD so tests provide continuous feedback.

𝟲. 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿 & 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲
Track failures, remove flaky tests, maintain the framework, and adapt as the product changes.

Because automation isn't successful just because you have hundreds of scripts.

It's successful when those scripts consistently give the team useful confidence.

The goal isn't:

It's:

Flaky Tests: The Coworker Who Says “Maybe” to Everything

Test run #102: ❌ Failed
Test run #103: ✅ Passed
Test run #104: ❌ Failed

QA: “So… is the build broken?”
Automation: “Maybe.” 😐😂

Flaky tests are dangerous because they slowly destroy trust in the test suite.

Once the team starts thinking, “That test is probably flaky,” a real failure can get ignored along with the noise.

The fix isn’t to keep rerunning the test until it turns green.

Investigate. Stabilize. Then trust the signal again.

Because a test suite that cries wolf 17 times a day eventually gets muted. 🐺🔇

content:
🎭 PLAYWRIGHT SERIES — DAY 4

⏳ Auto-Waiting & Assertions — Making Tests More Stable

One thing every automation tester has probably experienced:

“The element is there… so why did my test fail?” 😅

Sometimes the application is still loading, an element isn’t ready for interaction, or the UI hasn’t reached the expected state yet.

That’s where Playwright’s auto-waiting and web-first assertions become really useful.

🔹 Auto-Waiting

Playwright automatically waits for elements to be ready before performing actions.

Instead of adding unnecessary waits:

❌

await page.waitForSelector('#login');
await page.locator('#login').click();

We can simply write:

✅

await page.locator('#login').click();

Playwright waits for the element to satisfy the necessary actionability conditions before interacting with it.

🔹 Web-First Assertions

Assertions can also wait and retry until the expected condition is met:

await expect(
  page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Login' })
).toBeVisible();
await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);

This helps us avoid writing unnecessary timing logic into our tests.

💡 My takeaway

Stable automation isn’t about adding more waits.

It’s about having the right synchronization strategy. 🎯

What I liked while exploring Playwright today:

✅ Less manual waiting
✅ Cleaner test code
✅ Built-in retrying assertions
✅ Better synchronization
✅ Easier-to-read tests

Coming from Selenium, this is one of the areas I’m particularly interested in comparing through real-world examples.

These are the types of questions that test real-world QA skills, not just theoretical knowledge.

content:
Selenium to Playwright migration — Part 1
I started this project assuming the obvious approach: hand an AI the old Selenium framework, tell it to migrate to Playwright, done.

First session of my mentor Pramod Dutta's course talked me out of that in the first twenty minutes, with a ratio that stuck with me: 95% planning, 5% code writing.

The plan itself is a 4-phase rollout, not a one-shot conversion:

Pilot — pick 5-10 high-value test cases, stand up the new Playwright project with real conventions from day one.

Parallel Run & Baseline — keep the old Selenium suite running, add a Playwright CI job alongside it, and compare flake rate and duration between the two. Not a guess about whether the migration is better — actual data, side by side.

Scale Conversion — once that baseline holds up, new feature work goes Playwright-only, and you convert the flaky/slow Selenium tests first, since that's where migration proves its value fastest.

Sunset Selenium — retire the legacy suite only once coverage and stability thresholds are actually met, not before.

The detail that made it click for me: 
→"flaky" isn't a feeling, it's a number. 

→Run a test N times before labeling it anything — say 10 runs, 3 failures. 

→Only once you've quantified that can "deflaky after migration" mean something you can actually prove happened.


More from this series soon.

content:
Testing that starts late increases cost and delays releases.

To prevent this, embed testing activities in planning and design rather than leaving them for the end. Invite QA to backlog refinement, pair testers with developers on stories, and define small measurable acceptance criteria and lightweight exit gates.

Automate fast feedback on every pull request. Prioritize unit and integration tests that run in seconds to minutes. Add contract and targeted end-to-end tests to protect critical flows. Use feature flags to decouple deployment from release and to exercise behavior safely in production. Enforce CI pipeline gating and maintain reliable synthetic test data to avoid flaky results.

Focus testing on risk. Map features to business impact and concentrate exploratory and manual testing where automation cannot cover uncertainty. Track defect escape rate, mean time to detect, and lead time for changes so that improvements are measurable.

Make testing a team responsibility, not a phase. When everyone owns quality, defects are detected earlier and fixes are cheaper.

Takeaway: Shift testing left by integrating QA into planning, automating fast feedback, and measuring outcomes.

content:
AI can write 200 test cases before my coffee gets cold.
 
It still can't tell me if this failure is a real bug or just Tuesday.
 
That's the part nobody automated. Writing tests was never the hard problem. Reading a failure and knowing whether it's a genuine regression, a flaky environment, a timing issue, or someone's test data quietly rotting — that's the actual job.
 
AI generates coverage in seconds now. Confidence still takes hours.
 
So the backlog changed shape. Less "write more tests." More "why did 40 tests fail and only 2 of them mean anything."
 
We didn't remove the bottleneck. We just moved it from typing to triage.
 
The SDETs who'll matter most going forward aren't the ones prompting AI to generate suites. They're the ones who can look at a red pipeline and say, calmly, which 2 failures to actually worry about.
